From: marissa_cole@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Performance SLOs and scaling — follow up

Sam —

Great questions, and thanks again for the time yesterday. Below is a concise recap of what we discussed and the numbers you can use for the SOW. I'm also attaching a short matrix (redwood-slo-scaling-matrix.xlsx) that maps SLO bands to autoscaling behavior.

Recap / Recommended SLOs:
- Non-streaming generation (short prompts, tokens < 256): P50 = 120–180ms, P95 = 650–900ms on our standard dedicated tier.
- Streaming responses (chunked output): end-to-first-token P50 = 90–130ms, steady-state token latency P95 = 40–80ms (per-token).
- For long-context workloads (>= 2k tokens): add ~15–25% to P95 estimates depending on KV cache hit rate.

Throughput & concurrency guidance:
- Baseline throughput: 250 reqs/min (matches your baseline).
- Burst capacity: we support burst up to ~5x baseline for short windows (up to 10 minutes) with our warm-pool + pre-warmed workers. For your 1.2k reqs/min spikes, that maps to ~4.8x and is within typical burst behavior when warm pool is available.
- Concurrent open streams: we recommend supporting up to 400 concurrent streams on Dedicated with the recommended pool sizing (gives headroom for small growth).

Autoscaling / warm pools / queueing:
- Scale-up time (cold -> warm): ~60–120s to allocate GPUs and spin runtime (depends on region/image).
- Warm-pool behavior: we maintain pre-warmed workers that can attach to requests in <5s; configurable warm pool size (we typically recommend 15–25% of typical peak for settlement windows).
- Scale from warm pool to full capacity: additional nodes typically provision in ~30–90s (depends on cloud provider and instance type).
- Queueing: short requests are queued at edge for up to 12s before falling back to queued-worker lanes; for longer spikes we shift to measured-backoff and can route to a lower-cost model variant (graceful degradation) to preserve 99.9% availability while protecting latency SLOs.

Operational notes / tradeoffs:
- If you need hard P95 SLAs during large spikes, we suggest reserving Dedicated capacity for your top 2 settlement windows (minimum committed GPUs) and configuring a warm pool sized to expected spike shape.
- For cost-sensitive flows, we can set up automatic fallback to a quantized variant for non-critical requests — keeps availability while shaving cost.

Next steps I suggest:
1) Nikhil will share an SLA appendix + pricing for reserved warm pool sizing.
2) If you agree to reserve the baseline Dedicated nodes for the settlement window, we can run a 72-hour soak with synthetic spike tests to validate tail latency.
3) We'll schedule an ops runbook working session (30–45m) to agree queueing thresholds and degradation policies.

I'm happy to walk through the attached matrix with your infra team — would Thursday or Friday work for a 30m follow-up?

Best,
Marissa

--

Sam / Marissa —

Quick note from my side: attached is the SLA appendix and the proposed warm pool sizing for the SOW. Summary below for procurement copy-paste: 

- Recommended warm-pool size for 1.2k peak: 300 pre-warmed workers (approx. 25% of peak throughput; maps to ~6 reserved GPU instances on our m-optimized family with concurrency knobs).
- Soak plan: 72-hour run with synthetic traffic matching your profile; include 3x 1-minute microbursts each hour at 1.2k reqs/min and steady baseline 250 reqs/min. We will capture P50/P95/P99 per path and token-level latencies for streaming.
- Networking: pre-warmed instances sit in your VPC when using Redwood Private; if using Hosted/Dedicated, we require a small set of egress IPs to be whitelisted and a VPC peering config for data plane connection. Exact CIDR/ips provided after region selection.

I'll attach the SLA appendix and the scaling matrix shortly (redwood-slo-scaling-matrix.xlsx). Once you confirm, I'll open a procurement quote with the reserved warm-pool line item and DocuSign the SOW.

Next actions: 
- Sam: confirm soak dates (we have an ops window 5–8 Aug or 12–15 Aug).
- FinPay procurement: we'll send the DocuSign link when you say go.

Cheers,
Nikhil
